questions.question: Review dyspepsia, causes and symptoms. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Review dyspepsia, causes and symptoms.
  • The term Dyspepsia is used for a condition in which there is difficulty in digestion of
  • food. (I mark for definition)
  • Causes of Dyspepsia
  • • It can be caused by a number of conditions, like ulcers, gall bladder diseases,
  • pancreatitis, hepatitis and irritable bowel syndrome. The disease can occur due to
  • organic diseases of gastrointestinal tract, cardiovascular or kidney disease or
  • malignant disease.
  • • In the absence of organic reasons, rapid eating, inadequate chewing, swallowing air
  • through food, ingestion of undercooked foods or fried foods, gas forming vegetables,
  • protein-rich animal foods, absence of bulk in the diet produce the presence of air in
  • the stomach or intestine.
  • • The most common cause of dyspepsia is stomach acid. Acid can irritate the lining of
  • the stomach, oesophagus or small intestine, causing that familiar burning or painful
  • sensation.
  • • The major causes of dyspepsia are irregular food habits, heavy, late-night dinner, very
  • spicy foods, beverages and alcohol, excessive physical or mental strain, excessive use
  • of medicines, too much fried foods, sugars, sweets and starches, drinking excessive
  • fluids in between the meals causes bloating of the stomach.
  • (2 marks - ½ mark for each
  • point)
  • Symptoms of Dyspepsia
  • Symptoms of this disorder are bitter taste in the mouth, heart burn, nausea, loss of
  • appetite, distention, belching, anorexia, epigastric distress or pain, discomfort or pain in
  • the stomach, vomiting and cardio spasm. (2 marks if any eight listed)

questions.question: Discuss the role of dietary deficiency in liver damage. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Discuss the role of dietary deficiency in liver damage
  • • Fatty changes in liver in kwashiorkor may be due to low protein intake and reduced
  • capacity to produce lipoproteins.
  • • The liver is often grossly enlarged in children with kwashiorkor, containing 30-50 per
  • cent fat.
  • • Intrahepatic accumulation of fat results due to excess delivery of fatty acids to the
  • liver or enhanced lipogenesis.
  • • This is combined with impaired lipid transport from the liver secondary to apoprotein
  • deficiency. When protein is supplied fat clears from the liver.
  • • Fatty changes are common whenever there is high proportion of fat - in uncontrolled
  • diabetes, starvation, obesity and when too much CHO are infused through IV feed.
  • (1mark for each point)

questions.question: Explain the category I risk factors of CVD. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain the category I risk factors of CVD.
  • • Cigarette smoking – enhance endothelial damage, increase heart rate and BP,
  • increase LDL, decrease HDL, constrict blood vessel and promote thrombus formation.
  • • High saturated fat, high cholesterol diet – increase cholesterol, factor VII, and
  • atheroma formation. Saturated fat reduce LDL and VLDL receptor formation and
  • inhibit antiaggregatory prostacyclin.
  • • Elevated LDL – develops atherosclerosis
  • • Hypertension – leads to enhanced endothelial cell damage and target organ
  • involvement including retinopathy and renal insufficiency. Hypertension is associated
  • with obesity, blood lipid abnormalities, insulin resistance and glucose intolerance.
  • • Thrombogenic factors - leads to development of intracoronary thrombosis. High
  • fibrinogen concentrations, plasminogen activator-inhibitor I, platelet aggregability and
  • factor VII concentration increases leading to CVD. (All 5 points – 1 mark each)

questions.question: Explain the causes and symptoms of acute renal failure. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain the causes and symptoms of acute renal failure.
  • Causes
  • ● Loss of blood – as blood flow to kidney decreases in case of accidents, ulcers,
  • haemorrhages and at the time of delivery
  • ● Loss of plasma in burns and crush injuries
  • ● Loss of fluid in diarrhoea, vomiting, diabetic coma
  • ● General anaesthesia and surgical operations reduce renal blood flow
  • • Acute haemolytic disorders and Serious infections produce shock and reduce renal
  • blood flow ( 2.5 marks – ½ mark each for each
  • point)
  • Symptoms
  • ● Low urine volume as 20 – 200 ml/day
  • ● Increased serum urea nitrogen and creatinine due to accumulation of waste products of
  • protein metabolism
  • ● Increased serum potassium due to release from increased protein breakdown to
  • provide calories
  • ● Increased phosphate and sulphate with decreased sodium, calcium and base
  • bicarbonate
  • ● Lethargy, nausea, vomiting diarrhoea
  • ● Death due to potassium and water intoxication
  • (2.5 marks – ½ mark each for each point)

questions.question: Differentiate diverticulosis and diverticulitis. / [CO1] [5x4 = 20] Part D Essay Each question carries 10 marks
questions.solution_html:
• Differentiate diverticulosis and diverticulitis.
  • Diverticulosis Diverticulitis
  • Diverticulosis is the structural presence ofDiverticulitis is the inflammation or infection
  • pouches (diverticula) in the colon wall, often
  • found in people over 50.
  • of these pouches.
  • Diverticulosis is caused by pressure on weak
  • spots in the colon.
  • Diverticulitis occurs when these pouches
  • become inflamed, sometimes due to bacteria.
  • Diverticulosis is typically asymptomatic. Diverticulitis causes acute abdominal pain
  • (often lower-left side), fever, and nausea,
  • vomiting, and, rarely, bleeding.
  • Diverticulosis is managed by diet (high-fiber)
  • and, in some cases, lifestyle changes.
  • Diverticulitis requires medical intervention,
  • such as antibiotics, a liquid diet, or, in severe
  • cases, hospitalization and surgery.

questions.question: Explain haemodialysis and its dietary management. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain haemodialysis and its dietary management
  • ● Haemodialyser is used to remove waste from body and maintain the chemical balance
  • ● It consists of two compartments separated by a thin porous membrane
  • ● One compartment has patients blood and the other has the cleaning solution called
  • dialysate.
  • ● Plastic tubing attached to needles connect the patient to the machine
  • ● Smaller waste products like urea, creatinine and excess water is washed off.
  • ● The blood cells, protein and other required substances remain and enters the patients
  • body
  • ● Needed substances like calcium and dextrose can be added to dialysate.
  • ● Haemodialysis is performed with the help of an artificial fistula or graft.
  • (4 marks – 1/4 mark for each point)
  • Dietary management
  • ● Energy – 35 kcal/kg body weight
  • ● Protein – 1.1 g/kg body weight
  • ● Dietary salt : 3-4 g/day
  • ● Potassium : 50-7- mEq/day
  • ● Phosphorus – 1 g/day
  • ● Water – according to urine output of patient (6 marks – 1 mark for each point)

questions.question: Explain the types, symptoms and dietary management in hypertension. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain the types, symptoms and dietary management in hypertension
  • Types
  • • Primary hypertension – when genetic predisposition causes hypertension
  • • Secondary hypertension – hypertension caused by medication or illness
  • • Essential hypertension – cause of hypertension is unknown
  • • Mild hypertension – diastolic pressure is 90 – 104 mm Hg
  • • Moderate hypertension - diastolic pressure is 105 – 119 mm Hg
  • • Severe hypertension – diastolic pressure is 120 – 130 mm Hg
  • (3 marks – ½ marks each for each point)
  • Symptoms
  • • Headache, dizziness, impaired vision, failing memory, shortness of breath, pain over
  • heart, gastrointestinal disturbance and unexplained tiredness, bulges and ruptures of
  • blood vessel wall of heart, eyes or kidney (2 marks – ¼ marl for each
  • point)
  • Dietary management
  • • Energy – 20 kcal/kg of ideal body weight for sedentary and 25 kcal/kg of body weight
  • for moderate worker
  • • Protein – 60 g/day is advised. In severe conditions 20 g as a temporary measure is
  • advised as per Kempners diet
  • • Fat – 20 g vegetable oil. Omega 3 helps in regulating blood pressure.
  • • Sodium – restricted to 2-3 g/day. Increased sodium may lead to increased hypertension
  • • Potassium – 3500 mg/day. Low level of potassium may retain sodium and water leading
  • to elevated BP (5 marks – 1 mark for each point).

  • Types
  • • Acute Cholecystitis - This can occur without stones mainly in critically ill patients or
  • when the gall bladder and its bile are stagnant.
  • • Chronic Cholecystitis - Chronic cholecystitis is long-standing inflammation of the
  • gallbladder. It is caused by repeated, mild attacks of acute cholecystitis.
  • (2 Marks – 1 mark for each type)
  • Causes/Risk factors
  • • Dietary factors – high fat diet over a long period of time, cholesterol rich foods, high
  • sugar and intake of refined carbohydrate, low fibre diet, rapid losing of weight.
  • • Metabolic factors - obesity, high waist hip ratio, insulin resistance, diabetes and
  • hyperlipidemia.
  • • Physiological factors - female gender, family history of gallstones on the mother's side
  • of the family, older age, pregnancy.
  • • Medical conditions - Crohn’s disease. (2 marks - 1/2 marks for each point)
  • Symptoms
  • Severe pain in upper right or centre of abdomen, pain that spreads to right shoulder or
  • back, tenderness over abdomen when it is touched, abdominal bloating, tenderness on the
  • upper-right hand side of the abdomen nausea, vomiting, fever, little or no appetite,
  • sweating, blood test may reveal a high white blood cell count.
  • (1 mark)
  • Dietary management
  • Principles of diet - Adequate calorie, protein, carbohydrate, low fat, moderate to high
  • fibre, adequate fluid. (1 mark)
  • Nutritional requirements
  • • Calorie –Consume only the required calorie to maintain a healthy weight.
  • • Protein –The recommended intake is 60 gm. Choose lean protein sources.
  • • Fat – Initially restrict fat to 20-30gm/day. When the patient can tolerate, gradually
  • increase to 50-60g/day. Fat should be less than 25-30% of total calories.
  • • Fibre – Include moderate fibre, which helps in digestion and reduce cholesterol
  • absorption.
  • • Vitamins – Supplement fat soluble vitamins.
  • • Fluid – Adequate fluid is essential to keep the bile thin. It helps prevent stagnation.
  • (3 Marks- ½ marks for each point)

questions.question: Explain the symptoms and dietary management of rheumatic heart disease. / [CO3] [10x2 = 20]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain the symptoms and dietary management of rheumatic heart disease
  • Symptoms
  • • Chest pain, excessive fatigue, heart palpitation, thumping sensation in the chest,
  • shortness of breath, swollen ankles, wrists or stomach. (2 marks)
  • Dietary management
  • • Energy – 1000 – 1200 kcal / day. In case of obese patients loss of weight helps in
  • better functioning of heart
  • • Fat- 20 per cent of total calories. PUFA to saturated fat ratio 0.8:1. PUFA promotes
  • esterification of cholesterol to easily utilisable forms like thromboxanes and
  • prostacyclins which prevent thrombus formation
  • • Carbohydrates – include complex carbohydrates. High CHO can increase triglyceride
  • levels. Restricting to 60 per cent of energy intake can reduce risk of CVD
  • • Protein – normal allowances are suggested. Animal protein is not suggested.
  • • Vitamin B6, B12, folic acid supplementation reduce CVD risk related to
  • homocysteine risk.
  • • Vitamin C is involved in regulating cholesterol metabolism and maintaining structure
  • of blood vessels. Vitamin C activates adrenals and reduce cholesterol
  • • Sodium – restricted to 1600 -2300 mg.
  • • Potassium and magnesium helps to relax muscles, keep a healthy tone and maintain
  • steady heart rate.
  • (8 marks – 1 marks/point)
